Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. The actor is renowned for his talent, admired by critics all over the world. — RENOWNED (adj) = nổi tiếng, được kính trọng (theo hướng tích cực); collocation "renowned for sth", đi với giới từ "for" chứ không phải "in/at".
2. The singer's scandal brought her notoriety for all the wrong reasons. — NOTORIETY (n) = tai tiếng, nổi tiếng theo hướng tiêu cực; collocation "gain/achieve notoriety"; đừng nhầm âm với "variety".

3. A famous actress lives under intense scrutiny, with every move closely watched and criticised by the press. — SCRUTINY (n) = sự soi xét kỹ lưỡng; danh từ không đếm được, không có số nhiều "scrutinies"; collocation "intense media/public scrutiny".

4. Many young fans try to emulate the lifestyle of their favourite influencer. — EMULATE (v) = noi theo, cố sánh bằng (thường bằng cách bắt chước); trang trọng hơn "imitate"; collocation "emulate sb/sb's success".

5. Fans often develop a parasocial relationship with an idol they have never actually met. — PARASOCIAL (adj) = (mối quan hệ) một chiều với người nổi tiếng; thuật ngữ tâm lý học, chỉ dùng cho quan hệ fan–celebrity một chiều.

6. For influencers who lack genuine talent, online fame is usually evanescent, disappearing as quickly as it appeared. — EVANESCENT (adj) = phù du, chóng tàn; văn phong học thuật/trang trọng; collocation "evanescent fame/popularity".
7. Society often places famous singers and actors on an impossibly high pedestal. — PEDESTAL (n) = bệ tôn vinh; cụm cố định "put/place sb on a pedestal", nghĩa bóng là tôn sùng quá mức.

8. The pop star's team pulled a publicity stunt purely to attract media attention. — STUNT (n) = chiêu trò gây chú ý truyền thông; collocation "a publicity stunt", "pull a stunt"; khác nghĩa với "stunt" trong điện ảnh (pha nguy hiểm).

9. Excessive idolisation of celebrities can give young people a distorted idea of real achievement. — IDOLISATION (n) = sự thần tượng hoá thái quá; chính tả Anh-Anh dùng "-isation"; collocation "the idolisation of celebrities".

10. A single brand endorsement from a global superstar can be worth a fortune. — ENDORSEMENT (n) = sự quảng bá, chứng thực thương hiệu; collocation "an endorsement from/by a celebrity", "a brand endorsement"; khác "sponsorship".

11. The tabloid press thrives on printing gossip about a public figure's private life. — TABLOID (n/adj) = báo lá cải; collocation "the tabloid press"; đối lập với "broadsheet" (báo nghiêm túc, khổ lớn).
12. The actor's only claim to fame is that he appeared briefly in one famous film. — CLAIM TO FAME (idiom) = lý do khiến ai đó nổi tiếng; thường dùng với sở hữu cách "sb's claim to fame".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: A famous singer's private life often differs quite significantly from the image that fans have constructed of them.
Band 8: What emerges behind closed doors is frequently at odds with the carefully curated persona that fans have projected onto a famous singer.
2. Band 7: Some celebrities cultivate a manufactured persona simply to satisfy public expectations.
Band 8: Rarely does a celebrity's manufactured persona bear much resemblance to their private conduct, so tightly is that image curated to satisfy public expectation.
3. Band 7: Social media has considerably lowered the barrier for ordinary individuals to achieve a degree of fame.

Band 8: While social media has undeniably democratised access to visibility, the ease with which ordinary individuals can achieve fleeting fame says little about how sustainable that fame actually is.
4. Band 7: Being relentlessly pursued by photographers must place an enormous psychological strain on a public figure.
Band 8: The relentless intrusion of paparazzi surveillance arguably exacts a psychological toll on public figures that is rarely acknowledged by those who envy their fame.
5. Band 7: Young people often emulate the behaviour of famous influencers without pausing to consider the consequences.
Band 8: Impressionable as they often are, young people frequently emulate an influencer's behaviour with little regard for the consequences that such imitation might entail.
6. Band 7: A celebrity's reputation can be irreparably damaged overnight as a result of a single misstep.
Band 8: So precarious is a celebrity's standing that a solitary misstep can unravel a reputation built over an entire career.
7. Band 7: Many companies offer substantial endorsement deals to celebrities in exchange for promoting their products.
Band 8: Brands increasingly channel considerable sums into celebrity endorsement deals, banking on a single famous face to outperform an entire conventional advertising campaign.
8. Band 7: Fame acquired through social media tends to be relatively short-lived.
Band 8: Fame generated by social media is often strikingly ephemeral, fading almost as rapidly as the algorithm that first amplified it.

passages.text: The relationships that audiences form with public figures they have never met are a peculiarly modern phenomenon, and one that has expanded enormously in recent decades. A teenager who watches a particular video-blogger every morning, a middle-aged football supporter who has followed a single player through three clubs, and an admirer of a long-dead author whose collected letters they have read three times over share something significant: each maintains an imagined connection with someone unaware of their existence. Such bonds are no longer fringe peculiarities. According to survey work by the Pew Research Center, more than half of adults in industrialised economies report feeling a sense of personal attachment to at least one media personality. The scale of the phenomenon, the author would suggest, makes its routine dismissal as a symptom of contemporary shallowness considerably harder to sustain.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: The concept that organises this field of study, the parasocial relationship, was introduced in 1956 by the American sociologists Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl, who were interested in how television viewers responded to the early hosts of talk programmes. Horton and Wohl observed that audiences treated these figures as if they were friends or neighbours, sending letters, offering advice, and grieving when the broadcasts ended. The original paper was descriptive rather than judgemental, and the authors were careful not to characterise such bonds as pathological. That caution, the author notes, has not always been preserved by later commentators, who have at times reduced the original concept to a synonym for unhealthy fixation.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: One body of more recent work has sought to recover the original neutrality. Professor David Giles, a media psychologist at the University of Winchester, has argued for some years that parasocial engagement is best understood as a normal extension of ordinary social cognition. Human beings, Giles points out, are equipped with finely tuned systems for tracking the intentions, moods and reliability of other people; these systems do not switch off when the other person is mediated by a screen. From this perspective, recognising a familiar face on television, anticipating a presenter's verbal habits, and feeling pleased when a long-running character makes a wise decision are continuous with the cognitive routines of everyday friendship, not a degraded substitute for them. Giles maintains, with what the author considers reasonable evidence, that the great majority of parasocial bonds are mild, benign, and integrated rather harmlessly into the rest of social life.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: A more sceptical reading has emerged from researchers who have focused on the era of social media. Professor Alice Marwick of the University of North Carolina has argued that the digital intimacy now cultivated between influencers and their followers differs in important respects from the older parasocial pattern. Where viewers of mid-century television talk shows had no realistic prospect of contact with the host, contemporary creators stage a constant theatre of accessibility, replying to selected comments, hosting live streams, and releasing what is presented as unguarded behind-the-scenes footage. The result, Marwick contends, is a deliberately manufactured impression of two-way relationship that the creators know to be largely illusory. She does not argue that all such interactions are exploitative, but she does insist that the asymmetry of power, attention and economic interest must be kept in view when these bonds are evaluated.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: A third position has been taken by the British sociologist Professor Chris Rojek, who proposes that contemporary celebrity should be understood as a partial replacement for older sources of collective meaning. As organised religion has declined and traditional community ties have weakened across much of the industrialised world, Rojek argues, individuals have looked elsewhere for figures around whom to organise admiration, identification and even grief. The remarkable public response to the death of a popular musician or actor, in this analysis, is not a peculiar deviation from rational behaviour but an intelligible attempt to find communal meaning in a society that has fewer shared rituals than it once did. The author finds parts of Rojek's account persuasive, while remaining cautious about its more sweeping claims; not every emotional response to a public figure carries this much sociological weight.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: Across these positions, an honest synthesis is possible. The author would suggest that parasocial bonds are best understood as a heterogeneous category rather than a single phenomenon. Many such bonds are, as Giles has long argued, harmless extensions of ordinary social life and need no further justification. Some, as Marwick warns, are cultivated under conditions of significant economic asymmetry and warrant a measure of consumer caution. A smaller number, on Rojek's reading, may carry communal and even quasi-religious significance, particularly around moments of collective mourning. To collapse these distinctions into either a wholesale defence of celebrity attachment or a wholesale critique of contemporary shallowness, in the author's view, is to miss what is genuinely interesting about the field.
passages.title: Knowing Strangers

passages.text: Two final caveats deserve mention. The strongest research on parasocial bonds remains observational, and the long-term consequences of heavy engagement with influencer culture, in particular, are still poorly mapped. There is also a generational dimension that complicates simple judgements: older critics of new media frequently underestimate the social texture that younger audiences experience through it, while younger enthusiasts may, in the author's observation, be slower than they should be to notice the commercial machinery operating quietly behind the surface impression of intimacy. The most defensible position on present evidence, in the author's considered view, is neither moral panic nor uncritical endorsement, but the kind of attentive, empirically grounded ambivalence that the better researchers in this field have already begun to articulate in their published work.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture closes our media-psychology strand — focusing specifically on parasocial relationships in the age of audio-first creator content. [pause:5s] The conceptual framework I'll draw on this morning is taken from the work of Professor Inka Nyström — that's N-Y-S-T-R-Ö-M, the O is an umlaut O, no hyphen, no apostrophe. Nyström's 2016 monograph reframed parasocial attachment from a passive-viewer model into what she calls "voice-intimacy theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal listener panel I'll reference today was first recruited in 2014 — sorry, let me correct that, 2013; the published descriptive statistics in 2014 covered baseline diary data collected throughout 2013. So whenever I refer to the Nyström baseline year, please record 2013. [pause:3s] Right. A quick tense-orientation note, because the methodology has shifted materially across a decade. Parasocial-bond research USED TO be conducted almost exclusively with retrospective questionnaires; NOW the field deploys mixed methods combining diaries with real-time experience-sampling pings on smartphones and physiological skin-conductance measures; and from 2028 a North-American consortium WILL be deploying continuous eye-tracking sensors in domestic settings. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT mixed-methods state — that is, diaries plus experience-sampling. [pause:3s] Moving to terminology. The phenomenon Nyström foregrounds — the perception of one-sided emotional intimacy felt by an audience member toward a media performer whose voice enters private routines — is termed "voice intimacy". Now, you'll meet related labels in the older literature: parasocial bond, mediated friendship, audience-attachment construct. These all gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Nyström's construct. The currently accepted scholarly term is voice intimacy — v-o-i-c-e intimacy. So when the older literature uses parasocial bond or mediated friendship, those are related but distinct constructs. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to address is what media psychologists call the "engagement intensity continuum". When researchers describe how an audience member's emotional investment in a host evolves, they sketch a graded continuum running from light entertainment listening through routine companionship to intense affective attachment. So, you know, you'LL see a commuter who streams an interview podcast during a drive — that's light entertainment. Or a listener who reorganises their morning routine around a daily host's release schedule — that's intense affective attachment. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the engagement intensity continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the cohort data — and pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely. Of the six hundred and thirty regular listeners we surveyed across four English-speaking markets last autumn, MOST said they would feel personal grief if their favourite host stopped broadcasting — roughly seventy-one per cent. Only a few — about ten per cent — described the host purely as background audio with no emotional weight, and some — nineteen per cent — placed themselves in a middle range. So intense investment dominates numerically, but the no-weight tail, though small, is theoretically important. [pause:3s] A second construct I want to flag is "voice ubiquity". This refers to the temporal pattern by which a host's voice enters the listener's private spaces — kitchen, car, bedroom, bathroom — multiple times daily across years. At our Westmarket listener panel, our team logged one hundred and twenty-six documented ubiquity profiles across the cohort during one six-month observation window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that frequent platform-hopping by listeners weakens parasocial attachment is, frankly, not supported. Most of the listeners in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic decline in attachment scores as the number of audio platforms they subscribed to increased. Quite the opposite — many displayed a stable or even rising attachment to a "primary host" across multiple platforms. So the older "fragmentation-erodes-attachment hypothesis" is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in the afternoon seminar. I want you to focus on the experience-sampling protocols specifically, not the future eye-tracking deployment or the legacy questionnaire-only instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: parasocial attachment is best modelled as voice intimacy, not passive viewing; the technical term for one-sided audio intimacy is voice intimacy; intense investment dominates the cohort at roughly seventy-one per cent; and the fragmentation-erodes-attachment hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'LL examine creator-side parasocial labour. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The phenomenon known as "cancel culture" — the rapid online ostracising of public figures over a controversial remark or past behaviour — has reshaped contemporary public discourse. In what follows, I examine its principal causes and argue that, despite some genuine benefits, the trend is on balance more harmful than helpful.

The underlying causes appear to be largely structural. What digital-ethics research tends to highlight is the role of algorithms in amplifying outrage: platforms reward emotionally charged content, which encourages rapid pile-on dynamics. In addition, parasocial relationships with celebrities — the illusion of personal intimacy created by Instagram and TikTok — transform perceived moral lapses into personal betrayals. Legitimate accountability demands therefore become entangled with viral indignation.

On the positive side, supporters argue that cancel culture has given marginalised voices a means to hold powerful figures accountable. Predatory executives and abusive celebrities who previously escaped scrutiny have, in several cases, faced public consequences; the early #MeToo movement is a notable instance. On this reading, the trend can be seen as a partial corrective to long-standing impunity.

However, the negative effects appear more substantial. Once a target is identified, the punishment imposed often seems disproportionate to the offence, and the absence of due process undermines fair debate. Media-studies research suggests that the resulting chilling effect discourages open discussion, particularly on contested social issues. The psychological toll on both targets and audiences is also significant, with anxiety and burnout widely reported.

To conclude, cancel culture is driven largely by platform design and parasocial dynamics rather than by any single ideology. Although it has occasionally enabled overdue accountability, its tendency toward disproportionate punishment and suppressed debate makes its overall impact, in my view, more damaging than beneficial.

Few cultural shifts have reconfigured public discourse as rapidly as "cancel culture" — the online phenomenon in which public figures are collectively ostracised over an offensive remark, surfaced misconduct, or perceived ideological transgression. Its causes are largely structural, and although it has produced moments of overdue accountability, its net effect on civic debate is, in my view, predominantly negative.

The underlying drivers lie at the intersection of platform design and parasocial dynamics. Digital-ethics research consistently shows that algorithmic systems privilege emotionally charged content, generating cascades of moral outrage that traditional media never could. So tightly are users now bound to celebrities through curated, intimate feeds that perceived moral failures register as personal betrayals — a hallmark of the parasocial relationships documented by media-studies scholars. What this commodification of intimacy produces, in effect, is a public ever-ready to convert grievance into collective sanction.

There is, admittedly, a genuine case for the trend's positive dimension. Cancel culture has, on several occasions, dismantled the impunity historically enjoyed by predatory executives, abusive directors and politically sheltered figures. The early phase of the #MeToo movement, for instance, channelled grassroots testimony into structural reform that conventional institutions had long resisted.

Equally important, however, are its corrosive effects. Punishments routinely outstrip the gravity of the original offence; due process is sidestepped; and the resulting chilling effect, well documented in surveys of journalists and academics, narrows the range of opinions that can be safely expressed. The psychological toll on targets — anxiety, burnout, suicidal ideation in extreme cases — and on bystanders is, by most accounts, substantial.

To conclude, cancel culture is driven less by ideology than by platform incentives and parasocial intensity. Although it has occasionally enabled overdue accountability, the absence of procedural safeguards renders its overall influence on public discourse, on balance, more damaging than beneficial.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. The actor is renowned for his talent, admired by critics all over the world. — RENOWNED (adj) = nổi tiếng, được kính trọng (theo hướng tích cực); collocation "renowned for sth", đi với giới từ "for" chứ không phải "in/at".
2. The singer's scandal brought her notoriety for all the wrong reasons. — NOTORIETY (n) = tai tiếng, nổi tiếng theo hướng tiêu cực; collocation "gain/achieve notoriety"; đừng nhầm âm với "variety".

3. A famous actress lives under intense scrutiny, with every move closely watched and criticised by the press. — SCRUTINY (n) = sự soi xét kỹ lưỡng; danh từ không đếm được, không có số nhiều "scrutinies"; collocation "intense media/public scrutiny".

4. Many young fans try to emulate the lifestyle of their favourite influencer. — EMULATE (v) = noi theo, cố sánh bằng (thường bằng cách bắt chước); trang trọng hơn "imitate"; collocation "emulate sb/sb's success".

5. Fans often develop a parasocial relationship with an idol they have never actually met. — PARASOCIAL (adj) = (mối quan hệ) một chiều với người nổi tiếng; thuật ngữ tâm lý học, chỉ dùng cho quan hệ fan–celebrity một chiều.

6. For influencers who lack genuine talent, online fame is usually evanescent, disappearing as quickly as it appeared. — EVANESCENT (adj) = phù du, chóng tàn; văn phong học thuật/trang trọng; collocation "evanescent fame/popularity".
7. Society often places famous singers and actors on an impossibly high pedestal. — PEDESTAL (n) = bệ tôn vinh; cụm cố định "put/place sb on a pedestal", nghĩa bóng là tôn sùng quá mức.

8. The pop star's team pulled a publicity stunt purely to attract media attention. — STUNT (n) = chiêu trò gây chú ý truyền thông; collocation "a publicity stunt", "pull a stunt"; khác nghĩa với "stunt" trong điện ảnh (pha nguy hiểm).

9. Excessive idolisation of celebrities can give young people a distorted idea of real achievement. — IDOLISATION (n) = sự thần tượng hoá thái quá; chính tả Anh-Anh dùng "-isation"; collocation "the idolisation of celebrities".

10. A single brand endorsement from a global superstar can be worth a fortune. — ENDORSEMENT (n) = sự quảng bá, chứng thực thương hiệu; collocation "an endorsement from/by a celebrity", "a brand endorsement"; khác "sponsorship".

11. The tabloid press thrives on printing gossip about a public figure's private life. — TABLOID (n/adj) = báo lá cải; collocation "the tabloid press"; đối lập với "broadsheet" (báo nghiêm túc, khổ lớn).
12. The actor's only claim to fame is that he appeared briefly in one famous film. — CLAIM TO FAME (idiom) = lý do khiến ai đó nổi tiếng; thường dùng với sở hữu cách "sb's claim to fame".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: A famous singer's private life often differs quite significantly from the image that fans have constructed of them.
Band 8: What emerges behind closed doors is frequently at odds with the carefully curated persona that fans have projected onto a famous singer.
2. Band 7: Some celebrities cultivate a manufactured persona simply to satisfy public expectations.
Band 8: Rarely does a celebrity's manufactured persona bear much resemblance to their private conduct, so tightly is that image curated to satisfy public expectation.
3. Band 7: Social media has considerably lowered the barrier for ordinary individuals to achieve a degree of fame.

Band 8: While social media has undeniably democratised access to visibility, the ease with which ordinary individuals can achieve fleeting fame says little about how sustainable that fame actually is.
4. Band 7: Being relentlessly pursued by photographers must place an enormous psychological strain on a public figure.
Band 8: The relentless intrusion of paparazzi surveillance arguably exacts a psychological toll on public figures that is rarely acknowledged by those who envy their fame.
5. Band 7: Young people often emulate the behaviour of famous influencers without pausing to consider the consequences.
Band 8: Impressionable as they often are, young people frequently emulate an influencer's behaviour with little regard for the consequences that such imitation might entail.
6. Band 7: A celebrity's reputation can be irreparably damaged overnight as a result of a single misstep.
Band 8: So precarious is a celebrity's standing that a solitary misstep can unravel a reputation built over an entire career.
7. Band 7: Many companies offer substantial endorsement deals to celebrities in exchange for promoting their products.
Band 8: Brands increasingly channel considerable sums into celebrity endorsement deals, banking on a single famous face to outperform an entire conventional advertising campaign.
8. Band 7: Fame acquired through social media tends to be relatively short-lived.
Band 8: Fame generated by social media is often strikingly ephemeral, fading almost as rapidly as the algorithm that first amplified it.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Rise of Micro-Influencers: Brands are shifting away from massive celebrities toward "micro-influencers" (people with smaller but highly engaged niche audiences) because they appear more authentic and relatable.
Cancel Culture: The modern internet phenomenon where a public figure is boycotted or ostracized entirely from their industry due to an offensive remark, past flaw, or scandal.

Parasocial Relationships: Social media platforms like Instagram and TikTok create the illusion of intimacy, making fans feel personally connected to celebrities, which can lead to severe emotional distress if the celebrity acts out of character.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Are Celebrity Salaries Justified?

Arguments FOR high salaries: Celebrities generate massive revenue for production companies, sports clubs, and brands through their unique, irreplaceable charisma; their careers are often highly evanescent (short-lived); they sacrifice their fundamental right to privacy.

Arguments AGAINST high salaries: The immense wealth highlights severe societal inequality when compared to essential workers like surgeons, firefighters, or teachers, whose societal contribution is objectively far more critical.
Topic: Celebrities as Role Models

Should they be responsible? (Yes): Celebrities wield immense influential power over impressionable youth who idolise them; therefore, they have a moral obligation to promote positive values, philanthropy, and healthy habits.

Should they be judged only on work? (No): An actor's or athlete's only job is to entertain or perform; placing them on a moral pedestal is an unrealistic expectation of the public, as celebrities are humans prone to flaws.
Topic: Privacy vs. The Public Eye
The Right to Privacy: Constant surveillance by paparazzi causes severe psychological trauma and compromises physical safety; fame should not legally strip a person of basic human rights.

The Price of Fame: Celebrities actively court the media and public attention to build their lucrative careers and secure endorsements; therefore, public scrutiny is an inevitable and accepted part of their job description.

Cue card
> Describe a celebrity whose public image differs from reality.
> You should say:
> - who the celebrity is
> - what their public image is
> - what they are actually like (or what you have learned)
> - and explain why this contrast is significant.
Prep notes (1 minute)
WHO: Keanu Reeves
IMAGE: stoic action hero, brooding
REALITY: documented philanthropy, train-seat etiquette, anonymous donations
LEARNED: parasocial bias = systematic
DATA: Giles (Mass Comm & Society, 2022) on parasocial bonds
Model answer (≈ 274 words)

The celebrity whose public image perhaps most strikingly diverges from his off-camera reality is Keanu Reeves — and I find the contrast genuinely instructive about how parasocial perception works in the modern media economy.

Cast repeatedly in roles of brooding stoicism — from Neo in The Matrix to the laconic John Wick — Reeves has accumulated a cinematic persona of almost mythic remoteness. Tabloids have, over the years, layered on the so-called "Sad Keanu" meme, and the prevailing public assumption seems to be that the man behind the screen is a withdrawn, possibly melancholic figure. Yet a remarkably consistent body of journalistic reporting — from The New York Times to a well-documented 2020 GQ profile — paints a fundamentally different picture.

The reality, as far as one can credibly reconstruct it, is that of someone strikingly grounded. There's the documented USD 75 million he reportedly donated from The Matrix profits to special-effects crews; there are persistent reports of him giving up his seat on the New York subway; and there's a habit of unannounced charitable giving to children's hospitals that has only surfaced years after the fact. None of this fits the brooding caricature.

What I find genuinely interesting isn't really Reeves himself, but what the contrast reveals. Giles, writing in Mass Communication and Society in 2022, has shown that parasocial bonds — those one-sided emotional connections audiences develop with celebrities — generate remarkably stable but largely fabricated mental models. We don't perceive celebrities; we perceive commodified projections of them.
So the lesson, frankly, isn't about Keanu Reeves. It's about epistemic humility. The personas we consume are, almost by definition, not the persons themselves.
Examiner follow-up questions
Could this contrast itself be a form of carefully managed branding?
Why do you think audiences are so invested in such gaps?
Has social media made these gaps wider or narrower?

Q1. Does celebrity endorsement meaningfully influence politics?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd argue the effect is real but probably overstated, and rather context-dependent.

Evidence: A 2023 study by Garthwaite and Moore in the Journal of Public Economics estimated that Oprah Winfrey's 2008 endorsement delivered Obama roughly one million additional primary votes; conversely, a 2024 Pew Research survey found that 71% of US voters say celebrity political endorsements have no effect on their choice. Vesa et al. (Political Communication, 2023) further showed that endorsements move younger and unaligned voters more than partisans.
Explanation: What this points to is a marginal-effects story — endorsements rarely shift committed voters but can tilt low-information ones, particularly in close races.
Link: So while celebrity influence isn't transformative, dismissing it entirely would also misread the data.

The effect is real but probably overstated. Garthwaite and Moore, in the Journal of Public Economics in 2023, estimated that Oprah's 2008 endorsement delivered Obama roughly a million additional primary votes. Yet a 2024 Pew survey found that 71% of US voters say celebrity endorsements don't influence them. Vesa and colleagues, writing in Political Communication in 2023, showed endorsements move younger and unaligned voters more than partisans. What this points to is a marginal-effects story — endorsements rarely shift committed voters but can tilt low-information ones in close races. Dismissing them entirely would misread the data.
Q2. Should celebrities retain a robust right to privacy?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd argue yes, and rather more robustly than current legal frameworks tend to allow.

Evidence: The European Court of Human Rights' 2004 ruling in Von Hannover v. Germany established a strong privacy precedent for public figures in private settings; more recently, a 2023 Journal of Communication study by Ouvrein found that 68% of A-list celebrities reported clinical-threshold anxiety symptoms linked to paparazzi intrusion.

Explanation: What this signals is that the libertarian "price of fame" argument tends to underweight the genuine psychiatric morbidity that follows from sustained surveillance — and overstates the consensual nature of public scrutiny.
Link: Fame, then, shouldn't function as a wholesale forfeiture of basic Article 8 protections.

Q3. Has social media genuinely democratised fame?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd say it has democratised access to fame, but not the underlying economics of it.

Evidence: TikTok's 2024 transparency report cited 1.5 billion monthly active users, with roughly 50 million creators earning some income; yet an Influencer Marketing Hub 2024 study found that the top 1% of creators capture around 80% of platform earnings. Abidin's 2023 New Media & Society paper described this as the "evanescence economy" — fame is accessible, but increasingly fleeting and precarious.
Explanation: What this suggests is a paradox: more people can briefly become famous than at any point in history, but stable creative careers are arguably harder to sustain than in the broadcast era.

T28 — CELEBRITIES & FAME
Lecture title: "Parasocial Bonds, Fame Trajectories and the Psychology of Cancel Culture"
1. Section Type
IELTS Listening — Section 4 (academic lecture in media psychology, ~3:00 minutes). Speaker: Dr Rina Halvorsen, Department of Media and Communication Studies. Note-completion + multiple-choice hybrid.
2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

the rising-and-falling arc of a celebrity's career

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas
The lecturer will explain why fans feel they "know" celebrities they've never met.
The fame trajectory — sudden rise, plateau, decline — may follow a predictable pattern.
Cancel culture will likely be analysed psychologically rather than morally.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Right, settling in for our final session on media psychology. Today's lecture sits at the intersection of three phenomena: parasocial relationships, the fame trajectory, and the curious modern ritual we call cancel culture. I'll argue these aren't three separate topics — they're one mechanism viewed from three angles.

> Let's begin with parasocial bonds. Coined by Horton and Wohl in 1956, the term describes the illusion of intimacy that audiences develop with figures they've never met. Television gave us this in modest doses; social media has industrialised it. When a vlogger addresses the camera in close-up, your brain — evolutionarily wired for face-to-face dyads — processes that interaction as reciprocal, even though it is anything but. Recent Oxford research finds that heavy Instagram users score on attachment scales toward influencers at levels comparable to those they record for close friends.

> This sets up the fame trajectory, which sociologist Joshua Gamson maps in three stages: ascent (rapid visibility, often evanescent), plateau (commodification, brand-building, intense scrutiny), and descent (irrelevance, scandal, or the now-familiar cancellation). Most celebrities, statistically, never leave the first stage — the one-hit wonders, the viral nobodies.

Now, while you study that boycott-recovery curve, let me add a strand that complicates my "one mechanism, three angles" thesis in a productive way — the role of the platform itself. I've been speaking as though parasocial bonds form between an audience and a celebrity, two human poles. But there's a third party in the room, and it isn't neutral. The recommendation algorithm is engineered to maximise watch time, and intimacy, it turns out, is extraordinarily sticky. [pause] So the very bond Horton and Wohl described is now actively manufactured and amplified by systems with a commercial stake in deepening it. Um, the platform is, in effect, a matchmaker that profits from the attachment and, later, from the spectacular rupture.

That reframing matters for cancel culture, because it suggests the outrage cycle isn't merely a spontaneous emotional response — it's monetised. There's research on what's sometimes called moral-outrage contagion showing that posts expressing indignation travel faster and farther than neutral ones, roughly seventeen percent more reach per moral-emotional word in one Brady and Van Bavel study. Well, if betrayal generates engagement, and engagement generates revenue, then the architecture has a quiet incentive to keep us perpetually betrayed.

Let me introduce one counter-nuance, though, in fairness. Not every cancellation is irrational displacement of parasocial hurt. Some are straightforwardly the long-overdue accountability that older, gatekept media systems suppressed — think of the misconduct cases that only surfaced once audiences could organise around them directly. [pause] So we should resist the tidy cynicism of dismissing all of it as mob neurochemistry. The harder, more honest question is how to distinguish legitimate collective sanction from algorithmically inflamed pile-on — and that distinction is not one individuals can reliably draw in the heat of a feed. Which points us, inevitably, toward the design and governance of the platforms themselves, and that is the terrain I want us to step onto as we consider what, if anything, ought to be done…

> Which brings us to cancel culture. Psychologically, it's not primarily about justice. It's about betrayal. When a celebrity to whom audiences have parasocially bonded violates the imagined relationship — through a racist tweet, a hypocrisy, a moral lapse — the response mirrors the neural signature of personal betrayal, not abstract disapproval. That's why the rage feels so disproportionate to outsiders. We're not punishing a stranger; we're punishing someone we believed we knew. Now, observe figure four on your handout — the boycott-recovery curve since 2017…

The bar chart breaks down the average annual income of the top 100 celebrities in 2023 across five revenue streams, while the accompanying pie chart shows how tabloid scandal coverage was distributed in the same year.

Overall, brand endorsement dominates celebrity earnings, exceeding direct performance fees, whereas relationship-related scandals constitute by far the largest share of negative coverage. Together the two datasets suggest that public perception is shaped less by what celebrities are paid for than by what they are scrutinised for.

Regarding income, brand endorsements yielded an average of USD 28 million per celebrity — nearly a third of total earnings of USD 85 million and noticeably ahead of salaries at USD 22 million. Royalties, business ventures and social-media monetisation followed at USD 15 million, 11 million and 9 million respectively.

Turning to scandals, relationship and infidelity stories accounted for 36% of tabloid coverage, followed by substance abuse at 22% and financial scandals at 18%. Legal and political controversies trailed behind at 14% and 10% respectively. The contrast is telling: while endorsements reward a celebrity's public image, it is precisely their private conduct that attracts the heaviest scrutiny.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~200 từ)

The bar chart disaggregates the average annual income of the world's top 100 celebrities in 2023 into five revenue streams, while the pie chart shows how tabloid scandal coverage split across five categories that year.

Overall, two parallel concentrations stand out: earnings are weighted heavily toward brand endorsement, whereas negative coverage clusters around relationship scandals. The pairing implies that a celebrity's public worth and reputation are driven by different forces — commercial appeal and private conduct respectively.

By income, brand endorsements were the most lucrative stream, averaging USD 28 million per celebrity — close to a third of the USD 85 million total and six million ahead of salaries at USD 22 million. The remaining streams tapered off: royalties contributed USD 15 million, business ventures USD 11 million, and social-media a modest USD 9 million.

The scandal data display a comparable skew. Relationship and infidelity stories alone absorbed 36% of coverage, with substance abuse a distant second at 22% and financial scandals at 18%. Legal and political controversies trailed, at 14% and 10%. blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~284 words)

The phenomenon known as "cancel culture" — the rapid online ostracising of public figures over a controversial remark or past behaviour — has reshaped contemporary public discourse. In what follows, I examine its principal causes and argue that, despite some genuine benefits, the trend is on balance more harmful than helpful.

The underlying causes appear to be largely structural. What digital-ethics research tends to highlight is the role of algorithms in amplifying outrage: platforms reward emotionally charged content, which encourages rapid pile-on dynamics. In addition, parasocial relationships with celebrities — the illusion of personal intimacy created by Instagram and TikTok — transform perceived moral lapses into personal betrayals. Legitimate accountability demands therefore become entangled with viral indignation.

On the positive side, supporters argue that cancel culture has given marginalised voices a means to hold powerful figures accountable. Predatory executives and abusive celebrities who previously escaped scrutiny have, in several cases, faced public consequences; the early #MeToo movement is a notable instance. On this reading, the trend can be seen as a partial corrective to long-standing impunity.

However, the negative effects appear more substantial. Once a target is identified, the punishment imposed often seems disproportionate to the offence, and the absence of due process undermines fair debate. Media-studies research suggests that the resulting chilling effect discourages open discussion, particularly on contested social issues. The psychological toll on both targets and audiences is also significant, with anxiety and burnout widely reported.

To conclude, cancel culture is driven largely by platform design and parasocial dynamics rather than by any single ideology. Although it has occasionally enabled overdue accountability, its tendency toward disproportionate punishment and suppressed debate makes its overall impact, in my view, more damaging than beneficial.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~300 words)

Few cultural shifts have reconfigured public discourse as rapidly as "cancel culture" — the online phenomenon in which public figures are collectively ostracised over an offensive remark, surfaced misconduct, or perceived ideological transgression. Its causes are largely structural, and although it has produced moments of overdue accountability, its net effect on civic debate is, in my view, predominantly negative.

The underlying drivers lie at the intersection of platform design and parasocial dynamics. Digital-ethics research consistently shows that algorithmic systems privilege emotionally charged content, generating cascades of moral outrage that traditional media never could. So tightly are users now bound to celebrities through curated, intimate feeds that perceived moral failures register as personal betrayals — a hallmark of the parasocial relationships documented by media-studies scholars. What this commodification of intimacy produces, in effect, is a public ever-ready to convert grievance into collective sanction.

There is, admittedly, a genuine case for the trend's positive dimension. Cancel culture has, on several occasions, dismantled the impunity historically enjoyed by predatory executives, abusive directors and politically sheltered figures. The early phase of the #MeToo movement, for instance, channelled grassroots testimony into structural reform that conventional institutions had long resisted.

Equally important, however, are its corrosive effects. Punishments routinely outstrip the gravity of the original offence; due process is sidestepped; and the resulting chilling effect, well documented in surveys of journalists and academics, narrows the range of opinions that can be safely expressed. The psychological toll on targets — anxiety, burnout, suicidal ideation in extreme cases — and on bystanders is, by most accounts, substantial.

To conclude, cancel culture is driven less by ideology than by platform incentives and parasocial intensity. Although it has occasionally enabled overdue accountability, the absence of procedural safeguards renders its overall influence on public discourse, on balance, more damaging than beneficial.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nổi tiếng, được nhiều người biết đến và kính trọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He is a very **renowned** doctor, celebrated internationally for his groundbreaking medical research.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
're-' (lặp lại) + 'nown' gần 'noun/name' (tên) → tên được nhắc đi nhắc lại → nổi danh.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'for' để nêu lý do nổi tiếng: 'renowned for sth', không phải 'renowned in/at'.
vocabulary.definition_en: known or talked about by many people; famous and held in high esteem
vocabulary.definition_vi: nổi tiếng, danh tiếng (theo hướng tích cực)
vocabulary.example: He is a very renowned doctor, celebrated internationally for his groundbreaking medical research.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 're-' (lặp lại) + 'nown' gần 'noun/name' (tên) → tên được nhắc đi nhắc lại → nổi danh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tai tiếng — trạng thái nổi tiếng vì điều tiêu cực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some individuals even actively seek **notoriety** through outrageous behaviour just to stay relevant.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'notorious' (khét tiếng) + -ety → notoriety → tiếng tăm nhưng mang nghĩa xấu.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'notoriety' (tai tiếng) với 'variety' (sự đa dạng) — vần gần giống nhưng nghĩa khác hẳn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being famous for something bad; a widely known but negative reputation
vocabulary.definition_vi: tai tiếng, sự nổi tiếng theo hướng tiêu cực
vocabulary.example: Some individuals even actively seek notoriety through outrageous behaviour just to stay relevant.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'notorious' (khét tiếng) + -ety → notoriety → tiếng tăm nhưng mang nghĩa xấu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự soi xét, giám sát kỹ lưỡng, đặc biệt từ công chúng hoặc báo chí.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Living under intense public **scrutiny** means that a celebrity's every flaw is magnified by the press.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'scrutiny' nghe như 'scrub' (chà kỹ) → nhìn kỹ, xem xét từng chi tiết nhỏ.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ không đếm được, không có số nhiều 'scrutinies'; động từ tương ứng là 'scrutinise'.
vocabulary.definition_en: critical observation or examination, especially by the public or the press
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự soi xét, giám sát kỹ lưỡng
vocabulary.example: Living under intense public scrutiny means that a celebrity's every flaw is magnified by the press.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'scrutiny' nghe như 'scrub' (chà kỹ) → nhìn kỹ, xem xét từng chi tiết nhỏ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Noi theo, cố gắng sánh bằng hoặc vượt qua ai đó, thường bằng cách bắt chước.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Teenagers, in particular, fiercely desire to **emulate** the glamorous lifestyles they see online.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'emul-' gốc Latin 'aemulus' (đối thủ) → emulate → cố gắng sánh ngang, vượt qua đối thủ/thần tượng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'emulate' (noi theo để sánh bằng, thường trang trọng) với 'imitate' (bắt chước đơn thuần, trung tính hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: to match or surpass a person or achievement, typically by imitation
vocabulary.definition_vi: noi theo, cố gắng sánh bằng (thường bằng cách bắt chước)
vocabulary.example: Teenagers, in particular, fiercely desire to emulate the glamorous lifestyles they see online.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'emul-' gốc Latin 'aemulus' (đối thủ) → emulate → cố gắng sánh ngang, vượt qua đối thủ/thần tượng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mối quan hệ cận xã hội — một chiều, nơi người hâm mộ cảm thấy gần gũi với người nổi tiếng dù người đó không hề biết đến họ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Fans develop deep **parasocial** relationships with these figures, feeling a false sense of intimacy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'para-' (bên cạnh, giả) + 'social' (xã hội) → mối quan hệ 'giả xã hội', chỉ có một phía cảm nhận.
vocabulary.common_error: Thuật ngữ tâm lý học chuyên ngành; chỉ dùng để mô tả mối quan hệ một chiều (fan-celebrity), không dùng cho quan hệ hai chiều thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to a one-sided psychological relationship in which a fan feels an intimate connection to a celebrity who is unaware of them
vocabulary.definition_vi: (mối quan hệ) cận xã hội, một chiều với người nổi tiếng
vocabulary.example: Fans develop deep parasocial relationships with these figures, feeling a false sense of intimacy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'para-' (bên cạnh, giả) + 'social' (xã hội) → mối quan hệ 'giả xã hội', chỉ có một phía cảm nhận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phù du, chóng tàn — nhanh chóng biến mất khỏi tầm nhìn, ký ức hoặc sự tồn tại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> For those who lack true talent, the spotlight is incredibly **evanescent**, fading as quickly as it arrived.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'vanish' (biến mất) ẩn trong 'evanescent' → thứ gì đó sắp biến mất, chỉ thoáng qua.
vocabulary.common_error: Từ văn chương/học thuật cao, ít dùng trong văn nói hàng ngày; đừng nhầm với 'evasive' (né tránh).
vocabulary.definition_en: soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; fleeting and short-lived
vocabulary.definition_vi: phù du, chóng tàn, thoáng qua
vocabulary.example: For those who lack true talent, the spotlight is incredibly evanescent, fading as quickly as it arrived.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'vanish' (biến mất) ẩn trong 'evanescent' → thứ gì đó sắp biến mất, chỉ thoáng qua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bệ tôn vinh — vị trí được ngưỡng mộ, tôn sùng một cách lý tưởng hoá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We place renowned actors and singers on an impossibly high **pedestal**, expecting them to be perfect role models.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'ped-' (chân, gốc Latin 'pes') → pedestal → bệ đỡ dưới chân tượng → nơi tôn vinh ai đó lên cao.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng trong cụm cố định 'put/place sb on a pedestal'; nghĩa đen là bệ đỡ tượng, nghĩa bóng là tôn sùng quá mức.
vocabulary.definition_en: a position of being greatly admired or respected; an idealised, elevated status
vocabulary.definition_vi: bệ (tôn vinh); vị trí được tôn sùng
vocabulary.example: We place renowned actors and singers on an impossibly high pedestal, expecting them to be perfect role models.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ped-' (chân, gốc Latin 'pes') → pedestal → bệ đỡ dưới chân tượng → nơi tôn vinh ai đó lên cao.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chiêu trò — hành động được dàn dựng, thường nhằm thu hút sự chú ý của truyền thông.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some celebrities resort to a cheap publicity **stunt** just to stay relevant in the public eye.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'stunt' nghe giống 'stun' (gây sốc) → hành động gây sốc để thu hút sự chú ý.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'a publicity stunt' (chiêu trò PR) với 'stunt' trong điện ảnh (pha nguy hiểm do diễn viên đóng thế) — cùng từ nhưng ngữ cảnh khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: an action displaying notable skill or daring, often staged deliberately to attract publicity
vocabulary.definition_vi: chiêu trò (thường để gây chú ý truyền thông)
vocabulary.example: Some celebrities resort to a cheap publicity stunt just to stay relevant in the public eye.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'stunt' nghe giống 'stun' (gây sốc) → hành động gây sốc để thu hút sự chú ý.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự thần tượng hoá — hành động ngưỡng mộ, tôn sùng ai đó một cách thái quá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **idolisation** of celebrities can distort young people's sense of what genuine achievement looks like.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'idol' (thần tượng) + -isation → idolisation → biến ai đó thành thần tượng để tôn thờ.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-isation' (idolisation), không phải '-ization' kiểu Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the act of admiring or worshipping someone excessively, treating them as an idol
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự thần tượng hoá
vocabulary.example: The idolisation of celebrities can distort young people's sense of what genuine achievement looks like.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'idol' (thần tượng) + -isation → idolisation → biến ai đó thành thần tượng để tôn thờ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự quảng bá, chứng thực — lời ủng hộ công khai cho một sản phẩm, thường đổi lại bằng tiền.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A single brand **endorsement** from a global superstar can be worth more than an entire film's salary.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'endorse' (ký xác nhận phía sau tấm séc) + -ment → lời xác nhận công khai ủng hộ một sản phẩm.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'of/from', ví dụ 'endorsement from a celebrity'; đừng nhầm với 'sponsorship' (tài trợ mang tính hỗ trợ tài chính rộng hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: a public statement of approval or support for a product, often made by a celebrity in exchange for payment
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự quảng bá, chứng thực thương hiệu
vocabulary.example: A single brand endorsement from a global superstar can be worth more than an entire film's salary.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'endorse' (ký xác nhận phía sau tấm séc) + -ment → lời xác nhận công khai ủng hộ một sản phẩm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phù du, ngắn ngủi — chỉ tồn tại trong một khoảng thời gian rất ngắn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Social media has made a certain kind of **ephemeral** fame achievable within a matter of days.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp 'ephemeros' (kéo dài một ngày) → ephemeral → chỉ tồn tại trong thời gian rất ngắn.
vocabulary.common_error: Trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai 'e-PHEM-er-al', không phải âm đầu.
vocabulary.definition_en: lasting for only a very short time; short-lived
vocabulary.definition_vi: phù du, ngắn ngủi
vocabulary.example: Social media has made a certain kind of ephemeral fame achievable within a matter of days.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'ephemeros' (kéo dài một ngày) → ephemeral → chỉ tồn tại trong thời gian rất ngắn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Báo lá cải — loại báo khổ nhỏ, thường đăng tin giật gân, tin đồn về người nổi tiếng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **tabloid** press thrives on exposing every detail of a celebrity's private life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'tablet' (viên nén nhỏ) gợi liên tưởng khổ báo nhỏ, gọn, dễ đọc lướt tin giật gân.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Tabloid' vừa là danh từ (tờ báo) vừa là tính từ ('tabloid journalism'); không nhầm với 'broadsheet' (báo khổ lớn, nghiêm túc hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: a newspaper with a small page size, typically characterised by sensational, gossip-driven stories
vocabulary.definition_vi: báo lá cải
vocabulary.example: The tabloid press thrives on exposing every detail of a celebrity's private life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'tablet' (viên nén nhỏ) gợi liên tưởng khổ báo nhỏ, gọn, dễ đọc lướt tin giật gân.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người có sức ảnh hưởng trên mạng xã hội, dùng lượng người theo dõi để định hướng dư luận hoặc quảng bá sản phẩm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many brands now prefer working with a single **influencer** over an expensive traditional advertising campaign.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'influence' (ảnh hưởng) + -er → influencer → người tạo ảnh hưởng, thường qua mạng xã hội.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là danh từ chỉ nghề nghiệp mới, không viết 'influencor'; phân biệt với 'influential person' (người có ảnh hưởng nói chung, không nhất thiết trên mạng xã hội).
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who has built a large online following and uses that platform to shape opinions or promote products
vocabulary.definition_vi: người có sức ảnh hưởng (trên mạng xã hội)
vocabulary.example: Many brands now prefer working with a single influencer over an expensive traditional advertising campaign.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'influence' (ảnh hưởng) + -er → influencer → người tạo ảnh hưởng, thường qua mạng xã hội.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bôi nhọ, phỉ báng — nói hoặc viết xấu về ai đó nhằm hạ thấp danh tiếng của họ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The actress was widely **vilified** in the press after the misunderstanding went viral.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'vile' (đê tiện, xấu xa) + -ify → vilify → khiến ai đó trông xấu xa trong mắt công chúng.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường ở dạng bị động 'be vilified', ít dùng chủ động; đừng nhầm với 'verify' (xác minh) — âm gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: to speak or write about someone in an abusively disparaging manner, damaging their reputation
vocabulary.definition_vi: bôi nhọ, phỉ báng
vocabulary.example: The actress was widely vilified in the press after the misunderstanding went viral.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'vile' (đê tiện, xấu xa) + -ify → vilify → khiến ai đó trông xấu xa trong mắt công chúng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Văn hoá tẩy chay — hiện tượng công chúng đồng loạt rút lại sự ủng hộ dành cho một người nổi tiếng sau phát ngôn hoặc hành vi gây tranh cãi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Cancel culture** can end a career overnight, sometimes without clear evidence or due process.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cancel' (huỷ bỏ) + 'culture' (văn hoá) → xu hướng công chúng đồng loạt 'huỷ bỏ' sự ủng hộ dành cho ai đó.
vocabulary.common_error: Là danh từ không đếm được, luôn viết thường trừ khi ở đầu câu; không chia số nhiều.
vocabulary.definition_en: the widespread practice of withdrawing public support for a public figure after they say or do something considered offensive
vocabulary.definition_vi: văn hoá tẩy chay (người nổi tiếng)
vocabulary.example: Cancel culture can end a career overnight, sometimes without clear evidence or due process.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cancel' (huỷ bỏ) + 'culture' (văn hoá) → xu hướng công chúng đồng loạt 'huỷ bỏ' sự ủng hộ dành cho ai đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ảo giác về sự thân mật — cảm giác gần gũi giả tạo giữa người hâm mộ và người nổi tiếng mà họ chưa từng gặp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Social media deepens the **illusion of intimacy**, making followers feel as if they personally know a celebrity they have never met.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'illusion' (ảo giác) + 'intimacy' (sự thân mật) → cảm giác gần gũi giả tạo do truyền thông tạo ra.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm danh từ trừu tượng học thuật, thường xuất hiện trong nghiên cứu tâm lý về mối quan hệ parasocial, không dùng trong văn nói thường ngày.
vocabulary.definition_en: a false sense of closeness or personal connection, especially between a fan and a celebrity they have never met
vocabulary.definition_vi: ảo giác về sự thân mật (giữa fan và người nổi tiếng)
vocabulary.example: Social media deepens the illusion of intimacy, making followers feel as if they personally know a celebrity they have never met.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'illusion' (ảo giác) + 'intimacy' (sự thân mật) → cảm giác gần gũi giả tạo do truyền thông tạo ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cái tên quen thuộc — trở nên nổi tiếng đến mức ai cũng biết đến.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After the success of the movie, the young actor quickly became a **household name**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'household' (hộ gia đình) + 'name' → cái tên được nhắc đến trong mọi gia đình.
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định, không thêm mạo từ thừa hoặc chia số nhiều bất hợp lý: 'a household name', không phải 'household names' khi nói về một cá nhân.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person or brand that has become extremely well known to the general public
vocabulary.definition_vi: cái tên quen thuộc với mọi người, ai cũng biết
vocabulary.example: After the success of the movie, the young actor quickly became a household name.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'household' (hộ gia đình) + 'name' → cái tên được nhắc đến trong mọi gia đình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lý do nổi tiếng — thành tích hoặc sự kiện cụ thể khiến ai đó được biết đến.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> His only **claim to fame** is that he once met the President in a coffee shop.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'claim' (tuyên bố quyền) + 'to fame' → điều mà ai đó có thể 'nhận vơ' là lý do khiến họ nổi tiếng.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng với 'sb's' phía trước hoặc 'to' phía sau để nêu lý do cụ thể; không nhầm với 'claim' đơn thuần (tuyên bố).
vocabulary.definition_en: the specific achievement or event that makes a person known or notable
vocabulary.definition_vi: lý do khiến ai đó nổi tiếng
vocabulary.example: His only claim to fame is that he once met the President in a coffee shop.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'claim' (tuyên bố quyền) + 'to fame' → điều mà ai đó có thể 'nhận vơ' là lý do khiến họ nổi tiếng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quy tụ dàn sao — có sự tham gia của nhiều người nổi tiếng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It was a **star-studded** event attended by Hollywood's absolute elite.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'star' (ngôi sao) + 'studded' (đính, gắn đầy) → như bầu trời đính đầy sao → sự kiện đầy người nổi tiếng.
vocabulary.common_error: Tính từ ghép luôn có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ: 'star-studded event', không tách rời.
vocabulary.definition_en: featuring many famous performers or celebrities
vocabulary.definition_vi: quy tụ dàn sao, đầy sao nổi tiếng
vocabulary.example: It was a star-studded event attended by Hollywood's absolute elite.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'star' (ngôi sao) + 'studded' (đính, gắn đầy) → như bầu trời đính đầy sao → sự kiện đầy người nổi tiếng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vụt nổi tiếng, trở nên nổi danh, thường trong thời gian ngắn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She **rose to fame** overnight after winning the national singing competition.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'rise' (đi lên) + 'to fame' → đi lên đến đỉnh danh vọng.
vocabulary.common_error: Động từ bất quy tắc 'rise-rose-risen'; đừng nhầm với 'raise' (nâng lên, cần tân ngữ trực tiếp).
vocabulary.definition_en: to become famous, often suddenly or over a relatively short period
vocabulary.definition_vi: vụt nổi tiếng, trở nên nổi danh
vocabulary.example: She rose to fame overnight after winning the national singing competition.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'rise' (đi lên) + 'to fame' → đi lên đến đỉnh danh vọng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người chỉ nổi tiếng với một tác phẩm duy nhất rồi không lặp lại được thành công đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He was just a **one-hit wonder** in the 90s and hasn't released anything since.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'one hit' (một bản hit) + 'wonder' (điều kỳ diệu) → chỉ tạo được một điều kỳ diệu duy nhất rồi biến mất.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm danh từ ghép có gạch nối; luôn số ít khi nói về một người, thêm 's' ở cuối 'wonders' nếu nói về nhiều người.
vocabulary.definition_en: a performer, especially a musician, who achieves success with a single work but fails to repeat it
vocabulary.definition_vi: người chỉ nổi tiếng với một tác phẩm duy nhất
vocabulary.example: He was just a one-hit wonder in the 90s and hasn't released anything since.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'one hit' (một bản hit) + 'wonder' (điều kỳ diệu) → chỉ tạo được một điều kỳ diệu duy nhất rồi biến mất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trước công chúng — ở vị trí mà mọi hoạt động đều bị dư luận theo dõi, biết đến.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Living **in the public eye** means having absolutely no secrets from the media.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'public eye' (con mắt công chúng) → luôn bị nhìn, theo dõi bởi tất cả mọi người.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có mạo từ 'the': 'in the public eye', không bỏ mạo từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: in a position where one's activities are widely observed and known by the general public
vocabulary.definition_vi: trước công chúng, bị soi mói bởi dư luận
vocabulary.example: Living in the public eye means having absolutely no secrets from the media.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'public eye' (con mắt công chúng) → luôn bị nhìn, theo dõi bởi tất cả mọi người.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cái giá của sự nổi tiếng — những hệ luỵ hoặc sự đánh đổi đi kèm với danh vọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Constant intrusion and lack of privacy are simply **the price of fame** that celebrities must pay.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'price' (cái giá) + 'fame' (danh tiếng) → mọi vinh quang đều có mặt trái phải đánh đổi.
collocations: the price of fame is high
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom cố định với mạo từ 'the'; thường đi cùng động từ 'pay': 'pay the price of fame'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the negative consequences or sacrifices that come with being famous
vocabulary.definition_vi: cái giá phải trả của sự nổi tiếng
vocabulary.example: Constant intrusion and lack of privacy are simply the price of fame that celebrities must pay.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'price' (cái giá) + 'fame' (danh tiếng) → mọi vinh quang đều có mặt trái phải đánh đổi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hình mẫu, tấm gương — người được người khác noi theo về hành vi hoặc giá trị sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A good teacher naturally acts as a positive **role model** for young students.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'role' (vai trò) + 'model' (hình mẫu) → người đóng vai làm gương cho người khác noi theo.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm danh từ ghép, thường viết rời hoặc có gạch nối tuỳ phong cách; đi với giới từ 'for sb', không phải 'of sb'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person looked to by others as an example to be imitated, especially in terms of behaviour or values
vocabulary.definition_vi: hình mẫu, tấm gương
vocabulary.example: A good teacher naturally acts as a positive role model for young students.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'role' (vai trò) + 'model' (hình mẫu) → người đóng vai làm gương cho người khác noi theo.
